accuracy.reason: Models and capabilities are separated correctly; persistence, indexes and CAP limits agree with primary sources. Diagrams compare identical product data without implying exclusive capabilities.

evidence.quote: Categories describe common strengths, not exclusive capabilities.

mechanisms.reason: Connects representation to reads and duplicate updates; indexing and partition communication explain benefits and failures, beyond listing products.

evidence.quote: Keeping shared facts in one place reduces duplicate updates but can require joins at read time.

coherence.reason: Managed data leads to requirements, record and specialized models, overlapping features, costs and failure-aware selection. All eight card objectives support that progression.

evidence.quote: Connect each requirement to a data layout or capability, then name its write, storage, coordination or operating cost.

decisions.reason: Gives query and correctness criteria, one-store versus additional-store costs, and measurements that could overturn a choice.

evidence.quote: A separate service can still make sense when workload needs or operating limits justify it.

clarity.reason: Definitions and diagrams make the broad survey usable. Slide 4 compresses three specialized mechanisms, but explains every required concept without a missing prerequisite.

evidence.quote: An embedding represents an item as a list of numbers.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria: learner defines persistent operations, layout/application coupling and recovery limits; inventories records, access patterns, rules, growth, latency and operations; rejects category guarantees using slides 1-2 and 8.

All six criteria: slides 3-4 support rows/columns/joins, documents and duplicate-update cost, direct keys, query-driven partition grouping, graph traversal and numerical similarity with truth/equality limits.

All six criteria: slides 4-6 and 8 support overlapping spatial/vector features, measurement, additional-store coordination, index storage/write costs, duplication and distribution. Learner does not infer performance equivalence from feature names.

All six criteria: slides 7-8 support live isolated copies, completed-write consistency and request completion, partition-conditional conflict, operation/configuration dependence, requirement-to-cost reasoning and measurements that change a vendor-independent choice.

sourceChecks.claim: PostgreSQL concepts confirms managed relational records; PostgreSQL Backup and Restore explicitly calls for backups and explains recovery approaches.
PostgreSQL JSON Types confirms relational JSON support; MongoDB modeling links flexible records to application access patterns.
MongoDB modeling guidance connects embedding and references to read patterns and duplicate-update work; PostgreSQL concepts corroborates relational representation.
Cassandra logical modeling selects tables and partition keys from queries. Neo4j graph concepts confirms traversal; pgvector confirms approximate search trades recall for speed.
PostGIS documentation and linked Getting Started confirm its PostgreSQL extension; pgvector README confirms vector similarity in PostgreSQL.
PostgreSQL indexes introduction explains selective lookup and maintenance/space costs. Distribution and duplication costs are explicitly conditional design guidance.
FoundationDB CAP page distinguishes theorem availability from system availability; Gilbert-Lynch proof confirms the isolated-write/read conflict.
PostgreSQL concepts, Cassandra and MongoDB modeling support choosing representation from requirements. No universal performance or recovery guarantee is claimed.
